title: The Relief of Finally Naming the Problem
summary: "Communication issue" fixes nothing. Why a precise problem name cuts blame, points to a next step, and how to shrink a vague complaint to one sentence people can act on.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Third retro in a row, same complaints. Planning runs long. The spec changes after the sprint starts. PRs sit for two days. QA keeps finding the same kind of bug. Someone sums it up: "We have a communication problem." Everyone nods, someone suggests a new Slack channel, and the next retro sounds exactly the same.

Then one person asks a narrower question: "Who decides when the spec is final?" Nobody answers, because nobody does. The spec stays open until someone runs out of time. Now the problem has a real name: no one owns the decision to freeze the spec. You can almost hear the room exhale. Nothing is fixed yet, but for the first time everyone is looking at the same thing.

A problem well put is half-solved

That line is older than software. John Dewey wrote it in 1938, calling it "a familiar and significant saying," and then explained why it holds: "To mistake the problem involved is to cause subsequent inquiry to be irrelevant or to go astray." The way you frame a problem, he wrote, decides which ideas get considered, which get dismissed and which data you even look at (Logic: The Theory of Inquiry).

That's exactly what happened in the retro. "Communication problem" sent the team toward a new Slack channel. "No one owns the spec freeze" sends them toward an owner and a date. Same symptoms, different name, different next move.

Plenty of executives say their own companies struggle with this. In a survey of 106 C-suite executives from 91 companies in 17 countries, Thomas Wedell-Wedellsborg found that 85% agreed or strongly agreed their organizations were bad at problem diagnosis, and 87% said that flaw carried significant costs (Are You Solving the Right Problems?, Harvard Business Review). That's a self-reported survey. Still, when that many executives say it about their own companies, it's probably not just your team.

Some names make the fog thicker

A vague name feels like progress. It goes on the retro board, everyone agrees, and the problem looks handled while nobody touches it. Watch for these:

  • "Communication issue." Could be missing authority, unclear ownership, two teams with conflicting goals or simply no data. Each needs a different fix.
  • "Tech debt." Sometimes it's real debt. Sometimes it's a product question nobody has answered, and the code is just where the confusion shows.
  • "It's a design problem." Compare that with "users have to pick a plan before they can see what each plan includes." The second one points at a behavior, so people can bring examples.
  • "Process problem." Which step? Who's waiting on whom?

A useful test: could two people read the name and propose the same first step? If one hears "more meetings" and the other hears "fewer meetings," the name is still too blurry.

A good name takes the heat off people

When a problem has no name, people become the explanation. Design is slow. Engineering is too cautious. Product keeps changing its mind. Everyone defends their own frustration, and the conversation gets personal fast.

A precise name moves attention to the system those people work in. "Product keeps changing its mind" is about a person. "The spec has no freeze point, so late feedback always gets in" is about how the work flows. People can look at the second one together without anyone needing to defend themselves. A lot of the relief in the room comes from exactly that.

The right name hands you a next step

You can usually tell a good name by how obvious the next move becomes:

  • "No one owns the spec freeze": pick the owner and the freeze date for next sprint.
  • "We test against fake data that looks nothing like production": get a sanitized sample of real data shapes before arguing about estimates again.
  • "PRs wait because only one person can review the payments module": pair someone with that person for two weeks.

Notice that none of these is "have another meeting about it."

How to get from a vague name to a sharp one

The first name is usually too big or too emotional ("everything is chaos"). Write it down anyway, then shrink it with a few questions:

  • What behavior shows the problem? Something you could point to in a ticket, a PR or a calendar.
  • Where does it happen, and where doesn't it? If one team ships on time with the same tools, what's different there?
  • When did it start? What changed around then?
  • If it were solved, what would you see next sprint?

Then try to fit it into one sentence: "When this happens, that follows, and it costs us this much." For example: "When the spec changes after sprint start, we redo about a third of the tickets, and we've missed two release dates this quarter." Swap in your own numbers. If you can't fill in the last part, go collect evidence before you collect solutions.

The best names sound almost boring once you have them. Of course that's why we keep redoing work. Of course that's why the same discussion keeps looping. The work wasn't impossible. It was just blurry.

Try this week

  • Find one complaint your team repeats in every retro and ask "what exactly happens, and where?"
  • Rewrite it as one sentence: when X happens, Y follows, and it costs Z.
  • Check that two people would pick the same first step from that sentence.
  • Replace one "communication issue" on your board with something more specific.

faqs.q: Why does naming a problem help a team?
faqs.a: A precise name gives everyone the same thing to look at, moves attention from people to the system they work in, and usually makes the next step obvious. John Dewey put it as "a problem well put is half-solved."

faqs.q: What's wrong with calling it a communication problem?
faqs.a: It's too broad to act on. It could mean missing authority, unclear ownership, conflicting goals or missing data, and each needs a different fix. If two people would propose different first steps from the same name, the name is still too vague.

faqs.q: How do I make a vague problem statement specific?
faqs.a: Ask what behavior shows it, where it happens and where it doesn't, when it started and what you'd see if it were solved. Then write one sentence: when X happens, Y follows, and it costs Z.
